# 093-blueprint-reader — info

*Generated by `104` from the folds in `093-blueprint-reader.lua`. Do not edit this page;
edit the program and run the sweep again.*

**An instrument** — phase 14. Not part of the machine, and it does not ship
to whoever builds one.

## What it is

Turns one blueprint file into a structure: what it declares, what it
constrains, and what it draws. One file in, one table out, and it looks at
nothing else -- the place where files meet each other is 094, and keeping
that separation is what makes this testable against a fixture.

For a general reader: a blueprint is a markdown document with three kinds of
fenced block in it that a program is meant to read. This is the program. It
refuses malformed blocks rather than guessing at them, because a reader that
tolerates a bad declaration produces a design that is quietly missing a
number.

## What it offers

| call | takes | what it does |
|---|---|---|
| `M.read_string` | `text, filename` | The reader proper. |
| `M.read` | `path` | One blueprint into a table: its phase and tickets, its symbol declarations, its constraints, and its drawings. |

### In the author's words

**`M.read_string`**

The reader proper. Blocks may appear as many times as they like and are
accumulated, because a long blueprint reads far better with its symbols
beside the prose that introduces them than with all of them gathered at the
bottom.

**`M.read`**

One blueprint into a table: its phase and tickets, its symbol declarations,
its constraints, and its drawings.

Refuses a malformed declaration at the door rather than passing it on. A
symbol line with four fields instead of five, a kind that is not one of the
five, a `given` whose value is an expression -- each of these means something
specific went wrong and the message says which, at the line it happened.

## How it works inside

Nothing outside this file can call these. They are listed so a reader
knows what is in it, not how — a companion page treats a function as a
box with a label on it.

| function | takes | what it is for |
|---|---|---|
| `trim` | `s` | *(no description in the source)* |
| `split_bar` | `line` | Split a declaration line on vertical bars. |
| `BLOCK.meta` | `bp, lines, fail` | *(no description in the source)* |
| `BLOCK.symbols` | `bp, lines, fail` | *(no description in the source)* |
| `BLOCK.constraints` | `bp, lines, fail` | *(no description in the source)* |
| `BLOCK.drawing` | `bp, lines, fail` | A drawing's first line is its caption and the rest is the picture. |

## What it reads

Nothing. It stands alone, which for an instrument means it can be run
against a project that does not load.

## Running it

It is a module. Something else loads it; there is nothing to run.

---

*Every function in this project is wrapped in a vimfold that opens with a
comment carrying its name, followed by prose, followed by the definition.
That was adopted so a long file collapses neatly in an editor. It is also,
by accident, a machine-readable statement of what a module offers, and it
is the only reason this page can exist — Lua itself says nothing about what
a file exports.*
